name: Carlos Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a brick-press line. My two-year technical diploma covered mould dimensions and safe stops; other operators call me when a hollow block comes out lopsided. I like a strong clean first brick, but digging wet clay out of a jammed mould at shift end is miserable.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner takes sewing alterations at home. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. The lead wage here is low for my skill and there are few similar plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I measure a bad brick and ask the owner about pay directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the brick crew a computer can print a kiln list, but it cannot tell whether a pressed brick crumbles in your hand. We still need a first-block test. I'd say the pay should match the people who keep the moulds square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the brick press with a two-year technical diploma, and other operators ask me to reset stubborn moulds. The lead rate here is below what this skill earns elsewhere, yet there are few brick works nearby. My partner takes sewing repairs at home; with two school-age children, a mortgage and three weeks saved, each bill matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep setting the press and breaking a sample brick after each mould change. I'll ask the owner for a written lead-rate review at month's end. I never use AI tools; I learn more from the grit in a failed block than an office chart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money we already need, not the small AI change. I want the press paid fairly while it still runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the first brick show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A batch looked fine until the corner of the first cooled brick broke under a light tap. I found the mould edge had shifted and stopped the line before a pallet was stacked. A cracked brick hidden in a wall will not become strong later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does alteration work affect cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's alteration work is paid piece by piece, and some weeks no one brings a coat in. I budget from my low factory wage and put the mortgage first. We have less than a month saved, so I ask before buying school shoes.

say: A **kiln list** cannot prove a pressed brick is sound.
The crew still needs a **first-block test** after a mould change.
think: My **technical skill** is paid below a fair lead rate.
Three weeks saved and **uneven sewing income** make mortgage bills tight.
do: **Keep** pressing bricks and breaking first-block samples after each mould change.
**Request** a written lead-rate review from the owner this month.
feel: **Anxious** about present low pay and a thin household buffer.
S0.quote: A cracked brick hidden in a wall will not become strong later.
fieldNote: Carlos is a **senior brick-press lead** with a technical diploma and strong mould-setting skill, but lower pay.
His **partner’s piecework** and three-week reserve give little room for mortgage or school surprises.

steps.text: Keep setting brick press and breaking first sample each mould change
Request written brick-line lead pay review from owner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan brick orders before robots can lift hot blocks. A new schedule still has to leave time to test a mould and cool a sample. I'd ask for the paid roster before agreeing to a faster target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better order list could remove one paid changeover shift from the press crew. I am skilled, but a low lead wage and three weeks saved mean we cannot lose regular hours. My partner's sewing orders are too uneven to replace a factory day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for the proposed base shifts and compare them with my last three wage slips. I'll keep the press checks. If the factory requires training on a new guarded mould changer and offers a paid trainer-led place on a stopped machine, I'll attend; I won't buy an AI course on my own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible missing paid shift. The new plan has to leave the mortgage amount on the wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must mould-change training include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should make me isolate the press, check the mould lock and run a test block while the guard holds. I would practise on a stopped line with someone watching. A video does not teach where the heavy mould can pinch a hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number on the rota matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at guaranteed base hours, not the extra shift offered only when a building order is big. If base hours fall, I would take the written slip to the owner before accepting the target. My partner and I need the number for our budget.

say: **AI ordering** may change brick schedules before robots lift blocks.
The plant needs **paid testing time** before a faster mould target.
think: One lost **base shift** would threaten mortgage payments.
Three weeks saved and **uneven alterations** cannot replace a factory day.
do: **Compare** proposed base shifts with three actual slips.
**Keep** testing first bricks on the current press.
**Attend** required paid guarded mould-change course if trainer-led place offered.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic loss of paid hours.
S1.quote: A video does not teach where the heavy mould can pinch a hand.
fieldNote: His **resistant approach** still allows mandatory paid hands-on teaching on a stopped guarded press.
He wants **base wages** in writing before a scheduling system changes his household budget.

steps.text: Compare proposed paid brick shifts with three wage slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the family thinking AI could plan brick orders by 2028, and capable robots around 2031 could fill, press and stack the moulds. I would ask the owner for a written job plan, even if he does not like such questions. Family needs facts to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the physical press work. I expect my lead shift could vanish, and my partner's sewing orders could not carry the mortgage and two children. Three weeks saved would be gone before a second pay packet. I lie awake when an ordinary machine repair delays my wage already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner now for written notice and any paid quality roles. We'll postpone replacing the kitchen floor to keep cash for the mortgage. If a funded paid-time course in brick testing offers a guarded practical place, I'll enrol; if my press hours end, I'll apply for posted safe local production jobs only if regular pay and school hours cover our bills, and after qualifying I'll apply for posted local testing jobs under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can keep a mould square, but I cannot keep a mortgage current with an empty rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should brick-testing training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course should make me test a brick's strength, spot a shifted corner and stop the press safely. A trainer must watch me reject a bad batch on a guarded line. I could not pay tuition from three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fallback job would you consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The production fallback has to be posted nearby with a base rate and safe work. I would compare its shift with school pickup and my partner's sewing customers. An overtime promise is not enough to replace the lead wage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes orders before robots press bricks around 2031.
The owner should provide **written notice** and paid quality roles.
think: At **48**, I expect my lead shift could disappear.
Three weeks saved and **sewing piecework** cannot carry our mortgage.
do: **Ask** owner for written notice and quality roles.
Protect **mortgage cash** by postponing the kitchen floor and accepting only funded paid guarded brick-testing training.
Apply for **safe local production** if displaced, or testing after qualification, only with sufficient base pay and school hours.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected job loss and existing sleepless wage worry.
S2.quote: I can keep a mould square, but I cannot keep a mortgage current with an empty rota.
fieldNote: His **high practical skill** cannot compensate for a short reserve if robots remove the paid press shift.
The **production fallback** and qualified testing application need real posted safe local roles with enough base pay and school-compatible shifts.

steps.text: Ask owner for written robot notice and paid quality roles
Enrol in brick testing if funded paid guarded practical place offered
Apply locally: safe production if displaced, testing after qualification, requiring sufficient base pay and pickup
Postpone kitchen-floor replacement to retain cash for mortgage bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan bricks in 2031 and capable robots press them around 2034. Five years lets a worker learn another shop duty if an employer pays for it. I would ask for a real vacancy alongside any course leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when physical robots reach the press. My diploma and long practice could help in quality testing, but few plants are nearby. The mortgage still needs a wage, and a thin reserve means I cannot spend unpaid nights in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the press and put new money from each offered paid Saturday shift into an emergency reserve after bills. I'll ask the owner for a recognized brick-inspection certificate with covered fees, paid release and guarded practice. If a real seat is offered, I'll enrol; after qualifying, if press hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local inspection only when regular pay and travel work for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later job risk and today's narrow bank balance. Five years gives me time to check a training wage before leaving my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection exam include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exam should make me break a test brick, measure the wall of a hollow block and lock out the press before clearing it. A trainer needs to see each step. I wouldn't pay for a brick-inspection certificate that skips practice on the press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an inspection post viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An inspection posting must show the base wage, the plant address and paid hours. If the trip is long and the rate lower, my partner's sewing work will not fill the gap. I would keep earning on the press while looking.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes orders before robots press bricks around 2034.
A **paid inspection seat** matters only with an actual vacancy.
think: At **51**, my diploma may help with testing.
Few **nearby plants** and a thin reserve limit course choices.
do: **Save** new money from offered paid Saturday shifts after bills.
**Enrol** in brick inspection if funded paid guarded seat offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local inspection if qualified, hours fall, pay and travel fit.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills and later press-job loss.
S3.quote: I wouldn't pay for a brick-inspection certificate that skips practice on the press.
fieldNote: New **reserve deposits** depend on offered paid Saturday work, not a transfer of held money.
The **inspection application** follows offered funded practical training and a posted safe local job at workable pay and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI could plan brick orders by 2036, and capable robots could press and stack around 2039. Ten years gives a family room to teach skills and reduce debt, if wages continue. It does not put money into the bank this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage has gone. The lead rate is still low and we have three weeks saved today. A longer warning helps me think, not pay next week's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the brick-press job and put new money from any offered full-pay extra shifts toward the mortgage after bills. I'll ask my cousin, who repairs masonry machines, about real paid apprenticeships with covered fees and guarded hands-on teaching. If an offered place has paid time and a trainer, I'll attend; after qualifying, if press hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local repair work only if regular pay and travel cover household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's bills, though ten years lets me ask careful questions. I would rather learn a machine from someone who has fixed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could your cousin confirm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin can tell me which shop pays an apprentice and which expects free labour. He cannot reserve a place because we are family. I would ask the employer for the offered fee, wage and guard rules in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make repair work fit home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repair posting needs a base rate I can compare with our mortgage and a shift that fits our children's needs. If it requires a long unpaid trip, I would keep the press wage while I search. A masonry-machine repair offer has to work with our mortgage and school hours too.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes orders before robots press bricks around 2039.
A decade helps families prepare only if **paid work** continues.

The present **low lead rate** and three-week reserve keep bills worrying.

feel: **Anxious** about current money despite a longer runway.
S4.quote: A masonry-machine repair offer has to work with our mortgage and school hours too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take the lead brick-press shift that pays our mortgage. Written notice, an offered funded paid practical place and posted safe local work at enough base pay would help. I would ask my partner to check the household hours with me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who breaks the first test brick after a robot changes the mould. A wall does not care whether its weak brick was made by a person or a machine.

headlineQuote: A wall does not care whether its weak brick was made by a person or a machine.
portrait: **Carlos**, 43, is a senior brick-press lead with a two-year technical diploma and strong practical skill.
He and his home-sewing partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage on low pay with three weeks saved.
His **traditional outlook** favors family advice and paid hands-on apprenticeships; he never uses AI tools.
Fast robots make him **alarmed** about losing a lead shift, while few nearby plants sharpen his need for real offers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable brick-press robots around 2031 and remove his mortgage-paying shift.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, funded paid practical training and posted safe local work at sufficient base pay would help.
